title: WHEN THE WORLD CALLS EVIL GOOD, WILL YOU STILL FOLLOW JESUS?
paragraphs: WHEN THE WORLD CALLS EVIL GOOD, WILL YOU STILL FOLLOW JESUS?

The battle between culture and Scripture is not just happening in society. It is happening inside the hearts of Christians who desperately want to be accepted without betraying the Savior who died for them.
There is a moment in almost every Christian's life when following Jesus stops being comfortable.
It may happen at a family dinner, when someone you love asks why you believe what the Bible teaches.
It may happen at work, when everyone laughs at something you know dishonors God, and you have only a few seconds to decide whether to join them or remain silent.
It may happen while scrolling through Facebook, when a thousand voices celebrate something Scripture calls sin, and suddenly you feel the weight of being different.
Or perhaps it happens somewhere nobody can see.
Alone in your bedroom.
Phone in your hand.
A Bible collecting dust beside you.
You know what Scripture says. You know what your friends believe. You know what your heart wants.
And for the first time in a long time, you are afraid that choosing Jesus might cost you something.
Not necessarily your life.
Maybe your reputation.
Your relationships.
Your opportunities.
Your sense of belonging.
And then comes the question that has quietly broken the courage of countless believers:
What if following Jesus means the world will no longer accept me?
But there is another question, one that reaches even deeper.
What if the greatest danger is not that the world will reject you for following Jesus, but that you will slowly reject His words to keep the world from rejecting you?
Read that again.
Because this is not simply an article about culture.
It is about the invisible negotiations happening inside our souls.
It is about the things we excuse because everyone else excuses them.
The convictions we bury because we do not want difficult conversations.
The biblical truths we quietly edit because obedience has become inconvenient.
And it is about the astonishing grace of a Savior who does not abandon His people when they discover how easily their courage can collapse.
If you have ever felt caught between loving people and remaining faithful to Scripture, stay with me.
Because Jesus never commanded us to choose between truth and love.
He showed us what both look like when they meet.
And the place where they meet is far more beautiful, far more demanding, and far more costly than either the religious crowd or the surrounding culture often imagines.
Imagine standing in the courtyard of the high priest nearly two thousand years ago.
The night air is cold.
A charcoal fire burns.
People are talking in low voices while Jesus is being questioned inside.
And there, warming himself among strangers, stands Peter.
The same Peter who had confidently declared that he would never abandon Jesus.
The same Peter who had walked on water toward Christ.
The same Peter who had witnessed miracles, heard the Sermon on the Mount, and confessed that Jesus was the Messiah.
Now someone recognizes him.
"Thou also wast with Jesus of Galilee" (Matthew 26:69, KJV).
Suddenly, the cost of belonging to Jesus becomes painfully real.
Peter denies Him.
Another accusation follows.
Another denial.
Then another.
Until the rooster crows.
And according to Luke 22:61, something devastating happens.
"The Lord turned, and looked upon Peter."
Imagine that look.
The eyes of the One who had loved him.
The eyes of the One who had warned him.
The eyes of the One Peter had promised never to forsake.
Scripture tells us that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
The Bible does not record every thought passing through his mind. But it tells us enough to recognize the tragedy.
A man who genuinely loved Jesus had allowed fear to overcome his confession.
Peter's failure was not caused by a complicated philosophical argument.
He did not suddenly discover a more sophisticated interpretation of Scripture.
He was afraid.
And fear made denial seem safer than faithfulness.
How many of us know that feeling?
We may never stand in the courtyard of a high priest, but we know what it means to feel watched.
We know the pressure of being the only person in the conversation who believes something unpopular.
We know how tempting it is to soften the truth until nobody objects.
And sometimes we do not even need someone to threaten us.
The possibility of losing approval is enough.
But Peter's story does not end with his denial.
And thank God it does not.
Because if it did, some of us would have no courage to continue reading.
After the resurrection, Jesus meets Peter beside another charcoal fire.
In John 21, the risen Christ asks him three times whether he loves Him.
Three questions.
A wounded disciple.
A Savior who has conquered death.
Jesus does not pretend Peter's failure never happened. He calls Peter back into love, responsibility, and discipleship.
"Feed my sheep" (John 21:17, KJV).
Then Jesus tells him, "Follow me" (John 21:19).
That is grace.
Not permission to keep denying Christ.
Not condemnation that leaves a repentant disciple without hope.
Grace that restores a fallen man and calls him forward into costly obedience.
The Peter who once trembled before the accusations of bystanders would later boldly proclaim Jesus before hostile authorities.
When commanded not to speak in Jesus' name, Peter and John answered:
"Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye" (Acts 4:19, KJV).
And in Acts 5:29, the apostles declared:
"We ought to obey God rather than men."
Something had changed.
Peter had not become a man incapable of weakness.
He had become a man restored by Christ, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, and increasingly willing to suffer for the truth.
That is the kind of transformation the Gospel produces.
And it is the kind we desperately need today.
Because culture is always speaking.
It tells us what is fashionable, desirable, offensive, acceptable, successful, and shameful.
Sometimes culture reflects genuine moral insight.
Sometimes it exposes injustices that Christians themselves have neglected.
Sometimes it encourages generosity, human dignity, compassion, and concern for the vulnerable—things believers should recognize as consistent with biblical teaching.
But culture can also normalize greed, celebrate pride, trivialize sexual sin, reward cruelty, redefine goodness according to popularity, and treat personal desire as the highest authority.
And Christians must be humble enough to recognize something uncomfortable.
Not everything called Christian is biblical, and not everything criticized by Christians is sinful.
Some of our strongest opinions come from family traditions, political loyalties, social habits, personal fears, or the customs of our churches rather than from the Word of God.
That means faithfulness requires more than rejecting whatever is new.
It requires testing everything against Scripture, carefully understood.
Paul writes in Romans 12:2:
The Greek expression translated "be not conformed" is μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε (mē syschēmatizesthe).
It carries the sense of not allowing ourselves to be patterned according to the present age.
Paul then uses μεταμορφοῦσθε (metamorphousthe), meaning "be transformed."
Notice the contrast.
The Christian life is not merely about resisting external pressure.
It is about inward renewal.
God is not simply trying to make us people who disagree with society.
He is transforming us into people whose thinking, desires, decisions, and conduct increasingly reflect Jesus Christ.
And that matters because it is possible to oppose the surrounding culture while remaining profoundly unlike Jesus.
A person can defend biblical morality and still be arrogant.
A person can quote Scripture accurately and still enjoy humiliating others.
A person can condemn sexual immorality while secretly nurturing lust.
A person can denounce dishonesty while cheating customers.
A person can speak loudly about righteousness while neglecting the poor, mistreating family members, or refusing to forgive.
Jesus did not come to create a community of people who merely win arguments.
He came to save sinners, reconcile them to God, and make them His disciples.
When Scripture conflicts with culture, our first question should not be, "How can I defeat these people?"
It should be, "Lord, what are You teaching me, and how can I remain faithful to You?"
Because the Bible is not a weapon God gave us to avoid examining ourselves.
It is His Word, through which He corrects, teaches, rebukes, and trains us in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16–17).
And sometimes the person most in need of that correction is the one holding the Bible.
Consider the words of Isaiah 5:20:
"Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness."
In the Hebrew text, the prophet uses the words רַע (raʿ, evil) and טוֹב (ṭov, good).
The warning concerns the dangerous reversal of moral judgment.
But look carefully at Isaiah's wider message.
The prophet is not merely condemning people who hold unfamiliar social opinions.
He confronts greed, injustice, corrupt judgment, arrogance, and those who deprive the righteous of justice.
Isaiah's warning cannot faithfully be reduced to a slogan against people we dislike.
It is a summons for everyone, including God's own people, to stop distorting good and evil.
That means when culture praises something Scripture truly condemns, Christians must not redefine sin simply to make obedience easier.
But when Scripture exposes injustice, hypocrisy, cruelty, or prejudice within our own communities, we must not defend those things merely because they are familiar.
Our loyalty belongs to Christ, not to whatever makes our group comfortable.
And this is where many conversations become painful.
Someone asks, "Why can't Christians just accept everything people choose to do?"
Another person asks, "Why are Christians so judgmental?"
Someone else says, "If God is love, why would He ever tell anyone no?"
These questions deserve thoughtful, compassionate answers.
Not mockery.
Not panic.
Not slogans designed to end the conversation.
Because behind some of those questions are people who have experienced real rejection, spiritual abuse, family wounds, or religious hypocrisy.
Others are sincerely trying to understand why Christians believe moral truth is more than personal preference.
We should listen before assuming we know someone's heart.
But listening does not require surrendering our convictions.
And conviction does not give us permission to stop listening.
John 1:14 describes Jesus as "full of grace and truth."
In Greek, the phrase is πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας (plērēs charitos kai alētheias).
Grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Jesus embodied both perfectly.
When He encountered sinners, He did not treat their sins as imaginary.
Neither did He treat broken people as disposable.
Think of the woman at the well in John 4.
Her conversation with Jesus began with a simple request for water.
But soon He spoke directly into the complicated reality of her life.
He knew her history.
He knew her relationships.
He knew the truth she could not conceal.
Yet He continued speaking with her.
He offered living water.
He revealed Himself to her as the Messiah.
And the woman who came to draw water left her jar and went to tell others about Him.
Jesus did not need to humiliate her to tell her the truth.
And He did not need to deny the truth to offer her grace.
That encounter should change the way we speak to people whose lives or beliefs differ from ours.
They are not projects to conquer.
They are human beings made in God's image.
People with names.
Histories.
Families.
Questions.
Fears.
Wounds we may know nothing about.
We can disagree with someone's beliefs or conduct without denying their dignity.
We can refuse to affirm what Scripture identifies as sin while remaining patient, kind, honest, and genuinely concerned for their good.
We can maintain Christian convictions without cruelty.
And we must remember that the Gospel confronts every one of us.
Not merely the sins our communities find easiest to condemn.
Pride is sin.
Greed is sin.
Lust is sin.
Deceit is sin.
Hatred is sin.
Partiality is sin.
Self-righteousness is sin.
And every person who has ever fallen short of God's glory needs the mercy found in Jesus Christ (Romans 3:23–24).
There is no room at the foot of the cross for the illusion that we are saved because our sins are more respectable than someone else's.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our own works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the grace that saves us also teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live for God (Titus 2:11–14).
That is why the biblical response to cultural conflict cannot be either unconditional approval or contemptuous rejection.
It must be faithful discipleship shaped by Scripture and the character of Christ.
But how do we know when a cultural belief genuinely contradicts Scripture?
This question is more important than many Christians realize.
Because quoting a verse is not always the same as understanding it.
The Bible was written across different historical periods, languages, literary genres, and covenantal settings.
A command given to ancient Israel under the Mosaic covenant must be understood within the unfolding biblical story.
A proverb should not automatically be treated as an unconditional promise.
A historical description does not necessarily establish a moral command.
A passage must be read in context, with attention to its author, audience, purpose, and relationship to the teaching of Scripture as a whole.
Even original-language words require care.
Greek and Hebrew can clarify meaning, but they should never be used as decorations to make an unsupported interpretation sound authoritative.
Faithful interpretation does not begin with asking how we can make a verse support what we already want to believe.
It begins with asking what the inspired text actually communicates.
In Acts 17:11, the Bereans are commended because they examined the Scriptures to determine whether what they heard was true.
Their example matters.
Christians should not be afraid of careful questions.
If someone challenges our understanding of a biblical passage, we should be willing to study.
If we discover that we have confused a cultural tradition with a biblical command, humility requires correction.
If a difficult passage needs careful interpretation, intellectual honesty requires patience.
And if Scripture clearly teaches something that conflicts with our desires or society's expectations, discipleship requires obedience.
We do not honor God's Word by twisting it to avoid discomfort.
Neither do we honor it by pretending every disputed interpretation is equally certain.
There are essential doctrines Christians must faithfully confess, including the identity of Jesus Christ, His death and resurrection, salvation by grace, and His lordship.
There are also matters on which sincere believers differ in interpretation or application.
Romans 14 teaches us to handle certain disputable matters without despising or condemning one another.
Christian maturity includes learning the difference between a biblical command, a responsible inference, a matter of conscience, and a personal preference.
This distinction can prevent needless division.
But it can also expose the ways we sometimes hide behind the language of uncertainty because we do not want to obey what is clear.
And that is where the struggle becomes intensely personal.
Because perhaps the deepest conflict is not between Scripture and the world outside us.
Perhaps it is between Scripture and the world still living inside us.
The desire to be admired.
The hunger for approval.
The resentment we refuse to surrender.
The secret relationship we know is leading us away from God.
The dishonesty we justify because everyone in our profession does it.
The unforgiveness we protect because the person who hurt us never apologized.
The temptation to turn our faith into a public identity while keeping our private life untouched by repentance.
It is easy to speak about a culture that needs to change.
It is much harder to whisper:
"Lord, begin with me."
Jesus asks in Luke 6:46:
"And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?"
That question is difficult because it leaves little room for religious performance.
We may sing about surrender.
Post Bible verses.
Defend Christianity online.
Attend church.
Serve in ministry.
And still resist Jesus in the places where obedience would cost us something.
Christian faith is not proved merely by the convictions we announce.
It is expressed in the trust and obedience that flow from belonging to Christ.
Jesus said in John 14:15:
"If ye love me, keep my commandments."
He did not say that obedience purchases His love.
He taught that love for Him is inseparable from taking His words seriously.
And before we turn that verse into another burden for exhausted believers, remember who is speaking.
The Savior who loved His disciples.
The Savior who washed their feet.
The Savior who was preparing to lay down His life for them.
The Savior who would send the Holy Spirit to help them.
Christian obedience is not an attempt to earn the cross.
It is a response to the grace revealed through the cross.
So what happens when culture tells you to celebrate what Scripture forbids?
You do not have to become hateful.
You do not have to become theatrical.
You do not have to make every disagreement a public confrontation.
But neither must you violate your conscience or deny the teaching of Christ to secure acceptance.
You can speak truthfully.
You can explain your convictions respectfully.
You can refuse participation in conduct you believe is sinful.
You can continue showing kindness to those who disagree.
You can accept that some people will misunderstand you.
And you can remain open to correction where your own interpretation or behavior has been mistaken.
First Peter 3:15 calls believers to be ready to give a reason for their hope, with meekness and reverence.
Second Timothy 2:24–25 teaches that the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but should be gentle, patient, and able to teach.
These passages do not describe weakness.
They describe strength under the authority of Christ.
There is a difference between courage and aggression.
There is a difference between conviction and arrogance.
There is a difference between persecution for righteousness and criticism earned through unkindness.
If people reject us because we have faithfully followed Jesus, we may entrust ourselves to God.
But if they reject our cruelty, dishonesty, or contempt, we should repent rather than congratulate ourselves for being persecuted.
Jesus never promised that His followers would always be popular.
He also never gave us permission to be needlessly offensive.
The cross confronts the world, but it also crucifies our pride.
And there is something else we must understand.
We cannot faithfully follow Jesus while making political tribes, national identity, celebrities, social media influencers, or even religious leaders our ultimate authority.
Every human institution is capable of error.
Every cultural movement must be tested.
Every leader remains accountable to God.
Whenever allegiance to a movement requires us to excuse wrongdoing, distort Scripture, abandon compassion, or justify falsehood, we must remember whose name we bear.
We belong to Jesus Christ.
Not to an algorithm.
Not to a party.
Not to a crowd.
Not to an ideology.
Not even to the version of Christianity that makes us feel superior to everyone else.
Christ is Lord.
And His lordship reaches into our politics, finances, sexuality, relationships, entertainment, speech, ambitions, and treatment of the vulnerable.
There is no area of life where we can rightfully say, "Jesus, You may lead me everywhere except here."
Yet this is where grace becomes so precious.
Because every honest Christian eventually discovers areas where surrender remains unfinished.
Maybe you have been compromising.
Maybe you have been silent when love required courage.
Maybe you have spoken harshly when love required gentleness.
Maybe you have used biblical truth to wound people rather than to point them toward the Savior.
Maybe you have abandoned biblical convictions because you were tired of being misunderstood.
Maybe you have been so consumed with opposing the world that you have neglected prayer, compassion, holiness, and the people closest to you.
If any of that is true, do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The same Jesus who restored Peter still calls sinners to repentance.
The same Gospel that exposes our sin announces the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
The Greek word translated "confess" is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen).
In this context, it means acknowledging or confessing our sins before God.
Not managing our public image.
Not inventing excuses.
Not blaming the culture for everything we have chosen.
But coming into the light.
Telling the truth.
Receiving the forgiveness God promises through Christ.
And turning toward Him.
You may have compromised yesterday.
That does not mean you must compromise tomorrow.
You may have denied Christ through fear.
That does not mean your story must end in denial.
You may have used religion to cover pride.
That does not mean humility is beyond your reach.
You may have wounded people with your words.
That does not mean God cannot teach you to speak with grace.
There is forgiveness in Jesus.
There is power for change through His Spirit.
There is hope for the disciple who comes home.
But please do not misunderstand grace.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could become comfortable remaining enslaved to sin.
He died and rose again to reconcile us to God and bring us into newness of life.
The Gospel does not merely change our eternal destination.
It changes whom we belong to.
And because we belong to Jesus, the question is no longer simply, "What can I do without losing people's approval?"
It becomes, "What would faithfulness to my Savior look like here?"
Sometimes faithfulness means speaking.
Sometimes it means listening.
Sometimes it means refusing.
Sometimes it means apologizing.
Sometimes it means defending someone who is being mistreated, even when that person does not share your beliefs.
Sometimes it means admitting you were wrong.
Sometimes it means accepting a real cost rather than denying Christ.
And sometimes the bravest act of obedience happens when nobody else sees it.
Deleting what keeps feeding your temptation.
Returning money you dishonestly obtained.
Ending a pattern of deception.
Choosing purity when secrecy would make compromise easy.
Forgiving someone without pretending the harm was acceptable.
Opening your Bible before opening the app that has been shaping your thinking.
Praying for someone you would rather argue with.
These moments may never become viral.
But they matter to God.
And slowly, through His Word and Spirit, the Christian becomes less governed by the approval of the age and more formed by the character of Christ.
This is not an easy life.
Jesus never advertised it as one.
In Luke 9:23, He said:
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me."
The Greek phrase καθ᾽ ἡμέραν (kath' hēmeran) means "daily."
Not merely when the church music moves you.
Not merely when biblical values are socially popular.
Not merely when following Jesus brings encouragement and applause.
Daily.
When obedience is costly.
When temptation is private.
When relationships are complicated.
When you are misunderstood.
When you discover that faithfulness requires changing your own behavior before correcting someone else's.
Every day, the call remains.
But the One calling us is not a distant religious figure demanding sacrifice while remaining untouched by suffering.
He is the crucified and risen Lord.
He knows rejection.
He knows betrayal.
He knows false accusation.
He knows what it means to be abandoned.
He endured the cross, bearing our sins, and rose victorious over death.
And that changes everything.
Because the Christian's ultimate hope is not that culture will become more comfortable with Christianity.
Our hope is Jesus Christ Himself.
Cultures change.
Public opinion changes.
Laws change.
Platforms change.
Popular ideas rise and fall.
But the Lord who conquered the grave remains worthy of our trust.
And His Word continues to call every generation to repentance, faith, love, holiness, justice, mercy, and truth.
We are not called to hate the world.
We are called to love people in the world while refusing to be conformed to the sinful patterns of the age.
We are not called to retreat into self-righteous isolation.
We are called to be witnesses.
Salt and light.
People whose good works cause others to glorify our Father in heaven (Matthew 5:13–16).
And we are not called to measure faithfulness by how many people applaud us.
We are called to abide in Christ.
That is why this message matters beyond a single article.
There are people in your family who may never open a Bible but will read what you share.
There are friends who are quietly wrestling with their faith.
There are believers who are exhausted by the noise of cultural conflict.
There are people who have been hurt by religious hypocrisy and need to encounter the humility, truth, and mercy of Jesus.
And there are Christians who have been slowly compromising because nobody has lovingly reminded them that Christ is worth following even when obedience costs something.
Not to prove that you are better than anyone.
Not to shame people who disagree.
But to open a door for someone who needs to hear that biblical faithfulness and genuine love belong together.
Because it will not always feel easy to remember what matters most.
And sometimes we need to return to the truth before the voices around us become louder than the Word within us.
I also want to invite you to something deeper than reading one article and moving on.

Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and discover that no scandal, failure, or broken chapter is beyond the redeeming power of Jesus Christ.
Our mission is not simply to produce Christian content.
It is to keep pointing people toward the Savior who forgives sinners, restores the repentant, and transforms lives.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and spiritual nourishment accessible to people who need them.
And if you believe in that mission, I want to personally invite you to help sustain and expand it.
For Christians who prayerfully choose to give, such support can be an expression of generosity and an offering toward Gospel ministry.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly and cheerfully, not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
You can glorify God through prayer, faithful obedience, service, generosity, sharing the Gospel, and supporting trustworthy ministries according to your convictions and ability.
Those products are not the reason the Gospel matters.
They are simply another way to encourage faith, start conversations, and carry reminders of biblical truth into ordinary life.
The deeper invitation is to walk with us as we continue pointing people toward Jesus.
The love of Christ cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness is not a premium benefit.
Salvation is not unlocked by a monthly payment.
The gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord (Romans 6:23).
We invite support because ministry takes work and resources, not because God's grace has a price.
Let them encounter not merely another religious page, but an ongoing invitation to examine Scripture, consider the claims of Jesus, and grow in truth and grace.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something that deserves more than a quick reaction.
Where are you finding it hardest to remain faithful to Jesus right now?
Is it the fear of losing friendships?
The pressure to agree with everyone?
The temptation to compromise privately?
The struggle to speak biblical truth without becoming angry?
Or the painful realization that you have been defending Christianity publicly while resisting Christ privately?
You do not have to reveal details that should remain private.
Or share a testimony of how Christ has taught you to stand for truth while loving people who disagree with you.
Your words may encourage another believer who thought they were struggling alone.
We need more than loud Christian voices.
We need Christians whose lives make the character of Jesus visible.
Before we finish, return with me to that courtyard.
To the fire.
To the accusations.
To the frightened disciple who said he did not know Jesus.
Imagine if Peter's story had ended there.
A failed promise.
A broken man.
A bitter night.
But that was not the final chapter.
There was another fire.
Another conversation.
A risen Savior.
And a renewed calling.
Perhaps that is the word you need tonight.
Not another reason to despise the world.
Not another argument to win.
Not another excuse to compromise.
But a renewed invitation to follow Jesus.
To let Scripture correct you.
To let grace humble you.
To let truth steady you.
To let love govern the way you treat others.
To repent where you have fallen.
To seek forgiveness where you have wounded people.
To stand where faithfulness requires courage.
And to remember that your identity is not determined by the loudest voices in the culture.
It is found in the One who loved you and gave Himself for you.
So when the world and Scripture appear to disagree, do not rush to anger or fear.
Open the Word.
Study it faithfully.
Examine your assumptions.
Seek wise counsel.
Pray for discernment.
Listen carefully to the people affected.
Distinguish God's commands from human traditions.
And when you understand what faithfulness requires, obey Christ with humility, courage, and love.
Do not let culture become your Bible.
Do not let your traditions become your Savior.
Do not let fear become your master.
And do not let your defense of truth become an excuse to abandon the love that truth commands.
Because one day, the applause you worked so hard to preserve will be silent.
The arguments will be over.
The trends will be forgotten.
The people whose approval seemed so necessary will no longer determine what matters.
And what will remain is the Lord Jesus Christ.
The One who calls you.
The One who knows you.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose again.
The One whose grace is sufficient for every repentant heart that comes to Him in faith.
So choose faithfulness today.
Not because you are stronger than Peter.
But because the Savior who restored Peter is still worthy of your trust.
And if you have already failed, do not remain in the courtyard of your shame.
Come to Christ.
Confess the truth.
Receive His mercy.
And follow Him again.
The world may remember the moment you denied Him, but in Christ, your failure does not have to be the final word of your story.
